# 6. Cell visualization

**Module 06 — Cell visualization.**
In this module, we will visualize 2D and 3D single-cell graph plots using
pixelatorR's `cell_plot` visualization framework. This shows *where* proteins sit on a
single cell's surface graph and can help visualize clustering, polarization and colocalization patterns. The recipes need pixelatorR 0.23.0 or newer (`cell_plot_animate(boomerang = ...)` was added in that release). See the [cell visualization tutorial](https://software.pixelgen.com/pna-analysis/R/tutorials/cell_visualization/) for more detail.

```{r}
#| label: module06b_setup

library(here)
here::i_am("modules/06_cell_visualization.qmd")

source(here::here("modules", "common_setup.R"))

if (!exists("pg_data", inherits = TRUE)) {
  pg_data <- load_checkpoint("annotated_seurat_object.rds")
}
```

## 6.1. Parameters

> **Decision checkpoint**
> Set the cell type and markers to plot. In practice, cell visualization is an interactive process, where you select cells and markers of interest based on prior knowledge and/or analysis results and then plot them — often in multiple ways. The chunk below also sets colors, lighting, the output folder, and the cell-selection thresholds used by every figure.

As an example in this module, we will visualize CD8 T cells and in particular the markers CD82 and CD81. This is a pair of proteins which are known to often colocalize on the cell surface.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_parameters

cell_type_of_interest <- "CD8 T"           # one value from `cell_annotation`
markers_to_viz        <- c("CD82", "CD81") # pair inspected for colocalization
# One color per marker, in the same order as `markers_to_viz`. "Other" is added below.
marker_palette <- c("#E53E3E", "#3182BD", "#31A354", "#756BB1", "#E6550D", "#636363")
light_direction <- c(-1, 0.5, 1)           # shared lighting for the static renders
min_join_count <- 100                      # minimum observed joins for the pair
min_umi <- NULL                            # set a number to drop small fragments
out_dir <- here::here("results/06_cell_visualization")

if (length(markers_to_viz) < 2L || anyNA(markers_to_viz) || any(!nzchar(markers_to_viz))) {
  stop("`markers_to_viz` must name at least two markers.", call. = FALSE)
}
if (anyDuplicated(markers_to_viz) > 0L) {
  stop("`markers_to_viz` contains duplicate marker names.", call. = FALSE)
}
if ("Other" %in% markers_to_viz) {
  stop('`markers_to_viz` cannot include "Other"; that label is the background.', call. = FALSE)
}
if (length(markers_to_viz) > length(marker_palette)) {
  stop(
    "`markers_to_viz` has ", length(markers_to_viz),
    " markers, but `marker_palette` has ", length(marker_palette), ".",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}
if (length(light_direction) != 3L || !is.numeric(light_direction)) {
  stop("`light_direction` must be a numeric vector of length 3.", call. = FALSE)
}

# Names have to match the marker column. A hardcoded CD82/CD81 vector would
# paint the wrong proteins, or fail, after `markers_to_viz` is edited.
marker_colors <- c(
  "grey85",
  marker_palette[seq_along(markers_to_viz)]
)
names(marker_colors) <- c("Other", markers_to_viz)

# Cell-type labels such as "CD8 T" would otherwise become filenames with spaces.
viz_file_stub <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9._-]+", "_", cell_type_of_interest)
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Local proximity scores are log2 ratios. A symmetric limit keeps 0, the score
# of a neighborhood that matches the random expectation, at the middle of a
# diverging scale. Fixed limits such as c(-1, 1) paint every stronger
# neighborhood the same color.
lps_color_limit <- function(x) {
  values <- as.numeric(unlist(x, use.names = FALSE))
  limit <- suppressWarnings(max(abs(values), na.rm = TRUE))
  if (!is.finite(limit) || limit == 0) {
    return(1)
  }
  limit
}

# Shared selection filter. Both directions of an undirected pair can be
# returned; the chunks below keep one row per cell. A high log2 ratio on a
# tiny component is often a fragment, so `min_umi` can require a minimum
# component size. Leave it NULL to skip that filter.
colocalization_candidates <- function(object) {
  scores <- object |>
    subset(cell_annotation == cell_type_of_interest) |>
    ProximityScores(lazy = TRUE) |>
    filter(
      marker_1 %in% markers_to_viz,
      marker_2 %in% markers_to_viz,
      marker_1 != marker_2,
      join_count > min_join_count
    ) |>
    collect()

  if (is.null(min_umi)) {
    return(scores)
  }
  if (!"n_umi" %in% colnames(object[[]])) {
    stop("`min_umi` is set, but the object has no `n_umi` metadata column.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  scores |>
    select(-any_of("n_umi")) |>
    inner_join(
      tibble(
        component = colnames(object),
        n_umi = object$n_umi
      ),
      by = "component"
    ) |>
    filter(n_umi >= min_umi)
}
```

## 6.2. Select cells

How you pick a cell to visualize depends mainly on what you want to highlight in the visualization. It could be the spatial pattern on a typical cell, a polarized marker, a colocalization pattern, or a cell–cell conjugate. Often, it is therefore useful to filter or order the cells based on the colocalization score or a certain number of join counts, so that only cells with a certain level of colocalization and abundance would be included in the visualization.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_select_cells

# Highest colocalization score among cells that pass the shared filter.
# `component` breaks ties so the same table always selects the same cell.
sel_cells <- colocalization_candidates(pg_data) |>
  arrange(desc(log2_ratio), component) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)

cell_of_interest <- sel_cells$component
if (length(cell_of_interest) != 1L) {
  stop(
    "No '", cell_type_of_interest, "' cells passed the colocalization filter ",
    "(join_count > ", min_join_count, "). ",
    "Check `cell_annotation`, `markers_to_viz`, `min_join_count`, and `min_umi`.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

sel_cells
```

## 6.3. Visualization workflow

Once one or more cells have been selected, the next step is to visualize them. Most of the visualization recipes below follow a similar workflow.

- `RemoveCellGraphs()` drops graphs left by other analyses or visualizations, if needed
- `LoadCellGraphs()` reads CellGraphs for the cells that are to be visualized
- `ComputeLayout()` computes 3D coordinates according to a chosen layout method and stores them in the CellGraphs
- `ComputeLPS()` computes local proximity scores and stores them on the CellGraphs. Self-clustering (`mode = "self-clustering"`, the default) is a node-by-marker matrix in a layer. `mode = "all"` is one score per node in the node metadata
- `FetchLayoutData()` reads the coordinates and additional metadata from the CellGraphs
- `cell_plot()` and related functions create the visualization based on the fetched data

Each figure reloads the cells it draws, so the chunk can be run on its own after the parameter and selection chunks. Spectral layout stores coordinates under the name `spectral_3d`. `FetchLayoutData()` defaults to `wpmds_3d`, so every call below names `spectral_3d` explicitly.

## 6.4. Single cell - coloured by marker presence

A 2D projection of one cell, with the nodes colored by the presence of the first marker in `markers_to_viz`. On a PNA graph each node is one molecule, so that count is 0 or 1 and shows where the protein sits on the cell surface.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_marker_presence

marker_to_viz <- markers_to_viz[[1]]

# Counts are already on the graph, so this figure does not score neighborhoods.
pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cell_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral")

layout_counts <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cell_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = marker_to_viz,
  layer = "counts"
) |>
  mutate(node_value = .data[[marker_to_viz]])

p_counts <- layout_counts |>
  cell_plot(color = node_value, size = 0.7) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(colors = c("grey85", marker_colors[[marker_to_viz]])) |>
  cell_node_depth(focal_distance = 1.8) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction) |>
  cell_annotation(
    title = paste(cell_type_of_interest, "—", cell_of_interest),
    legend_title = marker_to_viz
  )

export_plot(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_", cell_of_interest, "_counts")),
  plot = autoplot(p_counts),
  width = 7,
  height = 6
)
```

The same plot recipe can be opened as an interactive 3D view. `cell_plot_interactive()` keeps the colors and the layout from the chunk above. Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. This chunk is left unevaluated so rendering the report does not open a widget. Run the figure first, then run this chunk when you want the viewer. The same is true of the other interactive chunks in this module.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_marker_counts_interactive
#| eval: false

p_counts |>
  cell_plot_interactive()
```

## 6.5. Single cell - coloured by local proximity score

The same cell, but now colored by the local proximity score of the first marker in `markers_to_viz`. This plot highlights the neighborhood where the proteins of the selected marker cluster. Passing `markers` stores self-clustering for that marker in the `lps` layer. Omitting `markers` would score every marker on the panel.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_marker_lps

marker_to_viz <- markers_to_viz[[1]]

pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cell_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral") |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = marker_to_viz)

layout_lps <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cell_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = marker_to_viz,
  layer = "lps"
) |>
  mutate(node_value = .data[[marker_to_viz]])

# A sequential palette hides the sign of a log2 ratio. The diverging scale is
# centered on 0 so depleted and enriched neighborhoods are distinguishable.
lps_limit <- lps_color_limit(layout_lps$node_value)

p_lps <- layout_lps |>
  cell_plot(color = node_value, size = 0.7) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(
    colors = c("blue", "white", "red"),
    limits = c(-lps_limit, lps_limit)
  ) |>
  cell_node_depth(focal_distance = 1.8) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction) |>
  cell_annotation(
    title = paste(cell_type_of_interest, "—", cell_of_interest),
    legend_title = paste(marker_to_viz, "LPS")
  )

export_plot(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_", cell_of_interest, "_lps")),
  plot = autoplot(p_lps),
  width = 7,
  height = 6
)
```

Again, the same plot recipe can be opened as an interactive 3D view.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_marker_lps_interactive
#| eval: false

p_lps |>
  cell_plot_interactive()
```

## 6.6. Single cell - multiple markers

Sometimes it can be useful to visualize several markers on the same cell. The `add_marker = TRUE` argument in `FetchLayoutData()` adds the protein identity of each node from the counts matrix. Nodes with no count are `NA`. `missing = "Other"` labels them as background even if that condition is missing, because `cell_plot()` drops rows whose mapped size or alpha is missing. The factor keeps the legend in `markers_to_viz` order; a character column would be sorted alphabetically.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_multi_marker

pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cell_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral")

layout_counts <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cell_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  add_marker = TRUE,
  layer = "counts"
)

p_multi_marker <- layout_counts |>
  mutate(
    marker = if_else(marker %in% markers_to_viz, marker, "Other", missing = "Other"),
    marker = factor(marker, levels = c(markers_to_viz, "Other")),
    highlight = as.numeric(marker != "Other")
  ) |>
  cell_plot(color = marker, size = highlight, alpha = highlight) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(colors = marker_colors) |>
  cell_node_scale_size(sizes = c(0.4, 3)) |>
  cell_node_scale_alpha(alphas = c(0.5, 1)) |>
  cell_annotation(
    title = paste(cell_type_of_interest, "—", cell_of_interest),
    legend_title = "Marker"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_", cell_of_interest, "_multi_marker")),
  plot = autoplot(p_multi_marker),
  width = 7,
  height = 6
)
```

Visualizing the cell as an interactive 3D view can reveal more details about the cell's structure and the distribution of the markers.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_multi_marker_interactive
#| eval: false

p_multi_marker |>
  cell_plot_interactive()
```

## 6.7. Single cell - multiple plots side by side

Here we show how to create and visualize local proximity scores for each marker separately and for the pair, on one cell. This involves two `ComputeLPS()` calls and two `FetchLayoutData()` calls. The first `ComputeLPS()` stores self-clustering of each selected marker in the `lps` layer. The second call, with `mode = "all"`, stores one colocalization score for those markers per node in the node metadata under the name `coloc`. See details of this in the [local proximity scores tutorial](https://software.pixelgen.com/pna-analysis/R/tutorials/cell_visualization/#local-proximity) or with the help of `?ComputeLPS`. `cell_grid()` arranges panels from one layout table. The two `FetchLayoutData()` calls return the nodes in the same order, so binding them by position keeps scores matched by node. Character panel labels are sorted alphabetically, which would put `coloc` and the markers in the wrong order, so `score_type` is a factor with the intended levels.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_cell_lps_panels

pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cell_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral") |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz) |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz, mode = "all", name = "coloc")

layout_lps <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cell_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = markers_to_viz,
  layer = "lps"
)
layout_coloc <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cell_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = "coloc"
)
if (nrow(layout_lps) != nrow(layout_coloc)) {
  stop(
    "Local proximity and colocalization layouts have different numbers of nodes, ",
    "so the scores cannot be matched by position.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}
layout_lps <- bind_cols(layout_lps, layout_coloc |> select(coloc))

score_levels <- c(markers_to_viz, "coloc")
layout_panels <- layout_lps |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_of(score_levels),
    names_to = "score_type",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  mutate(score_type = factor(score_type, levels = score_levels))

panel_limit <- lps_color_limit(layout_panels$score)

p_lps_panels <- layout_panels |>
  cell_plot(color = score, size = 0.6) |>
  cell_grid(cols = score_type) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(
    colors = c("blue", "white", "red"),
    limits = c(-panel_limit, panel_limit)
  ) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction)

export_plot(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_", cell_of_interest, "_lps_panels")),
  plot = autoplot(p_lps_panels),
  width = 4 + 3.5 * length(score_levels),
  height = 5
)
```

A grid visualization can also be opened as an interactive 3D view. Panels in a grid share one camera, so rotating or zooming one cell moves the others with it.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_cell_lps_panels_interactive
#| eval: false

p_lps_panels |>
  cell_plot_interactive()
```

## 6.8. Multiple cells - grid visualization

It can be very insightful to show the same scores across several cells. This can easily be achieved by creating a grid visualization. Set `n_cells` in this section to select the number of cells to visualize.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_grid_select

# Earlier figures drew one cell. Here we select the number of cells to visualize.
n_cells <- 4
if (length(n_cells) != 1L || !is.numeric(n_cells) || n_cells < 1) {
  stop("`n_cells` must be a single number greater than or equal to 1.", call. = FALSE)
}
n_cells <- as.integer(n_cells)

# One row per cell: the stronger direction of the pair, then the top scores.
grid_cells <- colocalization_candidates(pg_data) |>
  group_by(component) |>
  slice_max(log2_ratio, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(log2_ratio), component) |>
  slice_head(n = n_cells)

cells_of_interest <- grid_cells$component
if (length(cells_of_interest) == 0L) {
  stop(
    "No '", cell_type_of_interest, "' cells passed the colocalization filter ",
    "(join_count > ", min_join_count, "). ",
    "Check `cell_annotation`, `markers_to_viz`, `min_join_count`, and `min_umi`.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}
if (length(cells_of_interest) < n_cells) {
  warning(
    "Requested ", n_cells, " cells but only ", length(cells_of_interest),
    " '", cell_type_of_interest, "' cells passed the filter.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

# Column order is this rank, not the alphabetical order of component ids.
grid_cells <- grid_cells |>
  mutate(cell_label = paste("Cell", row_number()))

grid_cells
```

Creating a grid plot is straightforward. The layout needs a column for the cell and a column for the marker. `cell_grid()` uses those columns as columns and rows. Both are factors so the grid keeps the colocalization ranking and the order of `markers_to_viz`.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_grid

pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cells_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral") |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz)

layout_lps <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cells_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = markers_to_viz,
  layer = "lps"
)

cell_labels <- setNames(grid_cells$cell_label, as.character(grid_cells$component))
layout_grid <- layout_lps |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_of(markers_to_viz),
    names_to = "marker",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    marker = factor(marker, levels = markers_to_viz),
    # as.character() avoids factor indexing, which uses level codes rather than labels.
    cell_label = unname(cell_labels[as.character(component)]),
    cell_label = factor(cell_label, levels = grid_cells$cell_label)
  )
if (anyNA(layout_grid$cell_label)) {
  stop(
    "The layout contains components that were not in the selected cells.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

grid_limit <- lps_color_limit(layout_grid$score)

p_grid <- layout_grid |>
  cell_plot(color = score, size = 0.6) |>
  cell_grid(cols = cell_label, rows = marker) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(
    colors = c("blue", "white", "red"),
    limits = c(-grid_limit, grid_limit)
  ) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction)

export_plot(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_lps_grid")),
  plot = autoplot(p_grid),
  width = 2 + 3 * length(cells_of_interest),
  height = 1 + 3 * length(markers_to_viz)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_grid_interactive
#| eval: false

p_grid |>
  cell_plot_interactive()
```

## 6.9. Animations

Once you have found an interesting pattern of clustering or colocalization by using the methods described in this module, you might want to create an animated GIF of the cell(s). `cell_coord_rotate()` sets the axis and the turn angle, and `cell_plot_animate()` renders the animation. These chunks are left unevaluated so rendering the report does not spend time writing the GIF. Run them when you want the animation. `lock_light = TRUE` keeps the light fixed to the viewer while the cell turns; without it, the shading rotates with the cell and the turn is harder to see.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_animate_single
#| eval: false

pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cell_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral") |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz, mode = "all", name = "coloc")

layout_coloc <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cell_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = "coloc"
)
coloc_limit <- lps_color_limit(layout_coloc$coloc)

layout_coloc |>
  cell_plot(color = coloc, size = 0.7) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(
    colors = c("blue", "white", "red"),
    limits = c(-coloc_limit, coloc_limit)
  ) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction, lock_light = TRUE) |>
  cell_coord_rotate(axis = "y", max_degree = 360) |>
  cell_plot_animate(
    file = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_", cell_of_interest, "_rotation.gif")),
    frames = 120,
    fps = 20,
    width = 500,
    height = 500
  )
```

In the example below, we create an animated GIF of a grid of the same cells, colored by the local proximity scores of the selected markers. `boomerang = TRUE` plays the turn and then reverses it. `max_degree` in `cell_coord_rotate()` sets how far that turn goes. An odd `frames` count is raised to the next even number by pixelatorR, so this example uses an even count.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_animate_grid
#| eval: false

pg_data <- pg_data |>
  RemoveCellGraphs() |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cells_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral") |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz)

layout_lps <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cells_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = markers_to_viz,
  layer = "lps"
)

cell_labels <- setNames(grid_cells$cell_label, as.character(grid_cells$component))
layout_grid <- layout_lps |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_of(markers_to_viz),
    names_to = "marker",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    marker = factor(marker, levels = markers_to_viz),
    cell_label = unname(cell_labels[as.character(component)]),
    cell_label = factor(cell_label, levels = grid_cells$cell_label)
  )
if (anyNA(layout_grid$cell_label)) {
  stop(
    "The layout contains components that were not in the selected cells.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}
grid_limit <- lps_color_limit(layout_grid$score)

layout_grid |>
  cell_plot(color = score, size = 0.6) |>
  cell_grid(cols = cell_label, rows = marker) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(
    colors = c("blue", "white", "red"),
    limits = c(-grid_limit, grid_limit)
  ) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction, lock_light = TRUE) |>
  cell_coord_rotate(axis = "y", max_degree = 30) |>
  cell_plot_animate(
    file = file.path(out_dir, paste0(viz_file_stub, "_grid_rotation.gif")),
    frames = 30,
    fps = 15,
    boomerang = TRUE
  )
```
